prompt: Using the balance-sheet case study, explain why the authors say an average-score leaderboard can understate the real differences between models.

private.model_answer: Gemini scored 100% for $3.00 and Opus 95% for $83.05, a 27.7x difference. A leaderboard of average scores shows them as about equal, hiding that one delivers the same quality far more cheaply. On routine, well-specified wiring tasks, cost per correct output can differ enormously even when quality does not.

rubric.criterion: States that the two models reached similar high scores (about 100% vs 95%) at very different costs ($3.00 vs $83.05, or 27.7x)
Explains that an average-score ranking ignores cost, i.e. cost per correct output, so models that look equal can differ greatly
Mentions why Opus cost more (broad reads, large writes, many more output tokens) or that expensive models suit ambiguous or novel tasks
